claim: Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to the cognitive ability to attribute mental states to other individuals.
source: Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to the cognitive ability to attribute mental states to other individuals.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: The capacity to attribute mental states extends to animations featuring simple geometric shapes, such as the Frith-Happé animations.
source: This ability extends even to the attribution of mental states to animations featuring simple geometric shapes, such as the Frith-Happé animations in which two triangles move either purposelessly (Random condition), exhibit purely physical movement (Goal-directed condition), or move as if one triangle is reacting to the other triangle's mental states (ToM condition).
evidence: This statement is supported by established research on Frith-Happé animations and is cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Research on nonhuman primates regarding ToM has yielded inconsistent results.
source: While this capacity in humans has been thoroughly established, research on nonhuman primates has yielded inconsistent results.
evidence: This is a summary statement that references the state of the literature, supported by citations discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Both marmosets and humans exhibited longer fixations on one of the triangles in ToM animations, compared to other conditions.
source: We revealed that both marmosets and humans exhibited longer fixations on one of the triangles in ToM animations, compared to other conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from eye-tracking measurements presented in the study.

claim: Marmosets did not exhibit the same pattern of longer overall fixation duration on the ToM animations as identified in humans.
source: However, we did not observe the same pattern of longer overall fixation duration on the ToM animations in marmosets as identified in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing fixation durations between species.

claim: Both species activated extensive and comparable brain networks when viewing ToM versus Random animations.
source: Furthermore, our findings reveal that both species activated extensive and comparable brain networks when viewing ToM versus Random animations, suggesting that marmosets differentiate between these scenarios similarly to humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: Marmosets differentiate between ToM and Random scenarios similarly to humans based on neural activations.
source: Furthermore, our findings reveal that both species activated extensive and comparable brain networks when viewing ToM versus Random animations, suggesting that marmosets differentiate between these scenarios similarly to humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fMRI data showing comparable brain network activations.

claim: Marmosets' gaze behavior and neural activations indicate a distinction between ToM and non-ToM scenarios.
source: While marmosets did not mimic human overall fixation patterns, their gaze behavior and neural activations indicate a distinction between ToM and non-ToM scenarios.
evidence: This claim is supported by both eye-tracking and fMRI data presented in the study.

claim: Theory of Mind refers to the capacity to ascribe mental states to other subjects.
source: Theory of Mind (ToM) refers to the capacity to ascribe mental states to other subjects (Carruthers and Smith, 1996; Premack and Woodruff, 1978).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to foundational literature.

claim: Various experimental approaches have been devised to investigate the cognitive processes involved in ToM, including tasks involving text, non-verbal pictures, false belief, and silent animations featuring geometric shapes.
source: Various experimental approaches have been devised to investigate the cognitive processes involved in ToM, including tasks involving text (Happé, 1994), non-verbal pictures (Sarfati et al., 1997), false belief (Wimmer and Perner, 1983), and silent animations featuring geometric shapes.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to different experimental paradigms.

claim: Participants attribute intentional actions, human character traits, and even mental states to moving abstract shapes.
source: The latter approach is based on Heider and Simmel's observation that participants attribute intentional actions, human character traits, and even mental states to moving abstract shapes (Heider and Simmel, 1944).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heider and Simmel's foundational work.

claim: Animations featuring geometric shapes have been used to test the ability to ascribe mental states in autistic children.
source: Subsequent studies used these animations to test the ability to ascribe mental states in autistic children (Bowler and Thommen, 2000; Klin, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using animations with autistic children.

claim: In the Frith-Happé animations, a large red triangle and a small blue triangle move around the screen.
source: In the Frith-Happé animations, a large red triangle and a small blue triangle move around the screen (Abell et al., 2000; Castelli et al., 2002; Castelli et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the stimuli supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: In the Random condition of Frith-Happé animations, the two triangles do not interact and move purposelessly.
source: In the Random condition, the two triangles do not interact and move purposelessly, in the Goal-Directed (GD) condition the triangles interact but in a purely physical manner (i.e. chase, dancing, fighting and leading) and in the ToM condition the two animated triangles move as if one triangle is reacting to the other's mental state (i.e. coaxing, surprising, seducing and mocking).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: In the Goal-Directed condition of Frith-Happé animations, the triangles interact but in a purely physical manner.
source: In the Random condition, the two triangles do not interact and move purposelessly, in the Goal-Directed (GD) condition the triangles interact but in a purely physical manner (i.e. chase, dancing, fighting and leading) and in the ToM condition the two animated triangles move as if one triangle is reacting to the other's mental state (i.e. coaxing, surprising, seducing and mocking).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: In the ToM condition of Frith-Happé animations, the two animated triangles move as if one triangle is reacting to the other's mental state.
source: In the Random condition, the two triangles do not interact and move purposelessly, in the Goal-Directed (GD) condition the triangles interact but in a purely physical manner (i.e. chase, dancing, fighting and leading) and in the ToM condition the two animated triangles move as if one triangle is reacting to the other's mental state (i.e. coaxing, surprising, seducing and mocking).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Observation of ToM compared to Random animations activates brain regions typically associated with social cognition, including dorso-medial frontal, temporoparietal, inferior and superior temporal cortical regions.
source: Functional imaging studies have demonstrated that the observation of ToM compared to Random animations activates brain regions typically associated with social cognition, including dorso-medial frontal, temporoparietal, inferior and superior temporal cortical regions (Barch et al., 2013; Bliksted et al., 2019; Castelli et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2023; Gobbini et al., 2007; Vandewouw et al., 2021; Weiss et al., 2021; Wheatley et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to functional imaging studies.

claim: It remains uncertain whether other primate species share the capacity for spontaneous attribution of mental states to moving shapes.
source: Although the spontaneous attribution of mental states to moving shapes has been well established in humans, it remains uncertain whether other primate species share this capacity.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: There is evidence suggesting that monkeys can attribute goals to agents with varying levels of similarity and familiarity to conspecifics.
source: There is some evidence suggesting that monkeys can attribute goals to agents with varying levels of similarity and familiarity to conspecifics, including human agents, monkey robots, moving geometric boxes, animated shapes, and simple moving dots (Atsumi et al., 2017; Atsumi and Nagasaka, 2015; Krupenye and Hare, 2018; Kupferberg et al., 2013; Uller, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on goal attribution in monkeys.

claim: Some studies investigating the attribution of goals to inanimate moving objects in nonhuman primates have yielded inconclusive results.
source: However, the findings in this area are somewhat mixed, with some studies investigating the attribution of goals to inanimate moving objects yielding inconclusive results (Atsumi and Nagasaka, 2015; Kupferberg et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies with inconclusive findings.

claim: Human subjects exhibit longer eye fixations when viewing the ToM condition compared to the Random condition of the Frith-Happé animations.
source: While human subjects exhibit longer eye fixations when viewing the ToM condition compared to the Random condition of the Frith-Happé animations (Klein et al., 2009), a recent eye tracking study in macaque monkeys did not observe similar differences (Schafroth et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Klein et al., 2009.

claim: A recent eye tracking study in macaque monkeys did not observe differences in fixation patterns similar to those in humans for Frith-Happé animations.
source: While human subjects exhibit longer eye fixations when viewing the ToM condition compared to the Random condition of the Frith-Happé animations (Klein et al., 2009), a recent eye tracking study in macaque monkeys did not observe similar differences (Schafroth et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schafroth et al., 2021.

claim: A recent fMRI study conducted on macaques found no discernible differences in activations between ToM and random Frith-Happé animations.
source: Similarly, a recent fMRI study conducted on macaques found no discernible differences in activations between ToM and random Frith-Happé animations (Roumazeilles et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roumazeilles et al., 2021.

claim: Marmosets live in closely-knit family groups.
source: Living in closely-knit family groups, marmosets exhibit significant social parallels with humans, including prosocial behavior, imitation, and cooperative breeding.
evidence: This is a statement about marmoset social structure supported by established knowledge.

claim: Marmosets exhibit significant social parallels with humans, including prosocial behavior, imitation, and cooperative breeding.
source: Living in closely-knit family groups, marmosets exhibit significant social parallels with humans, including prosocial behavior, imitation, and cooperative breeding. These characteristics establish them as a promising nonhuman primate model for investigating social cognition (Burkart et al., 2009; Burkart and Finkenwirth, 2015; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on marmoset social behavior.

claim: Marmosets are a promising nonhuman primate model for investigating social cognition.
source: These characteristics establish them as a promising nonhuman primate model for investigating social cognition (Burkart et al., 2009; Burkart and Finkenwirth, 2015; Miller et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and inference from marmoset social characteristics.

claim: The study employed high-speed video eye-tracking to record eye movements in eleven healthy humans and eleven marmoset monkeys.
source: To directly compare humans and marmosets in their response to these animations, we employed high-speed video eye-tracking to record eye movements in eleven healthy humans and eleven marmoset monkeys.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The study conducted ultra-high field fMRI scans on ten healthy humans at 7T and six common marmoset monkeys at 9.4T.
source: Additionally, we conducted ultra-high field fMRI scans on ten healthy humans at 7T and six common marmoset monkeys at 9.4T.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: There was a significant interaction between species and condition for fixation durations (F(2,40)=13.9, p=<0.001, ηp2=0.410).
source: By conducting mixed analyses of variance (ANOVA), with factors of species (Human vs Marmoset) and condition (ToM vs GD vs Random animation videos), we found a significant interaction between species and condition (F(2,40)=13.9, p=<0.001, ηp2p2.410).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Humans showed longer fixation durations for ToM animation videos (M=432.6ms) compared to GD videos (M=279.9ms, p=0.008) and Random videos (M=308.2ms, p=0.01).
source: Here we observed longer fixation durations for ToM animation videos (M=432.6ms) as compared to GD videos (M=279.9ms, p=0.008) and Random videos (M=308.2ms, p=0.01) for humans (p=0.029) but not for marmosets (233.7ms for ToM videos, 219.6ms for GD videos and 235.6ms for Random videos, ToM vs GD: p=0.90 and ToM vs Random: p=1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: Marmosets did not show differences in fixation durations across conditions (233.7ms for ToM videos, 219.6ms for GD videos and 235.6ms for Random videos, ToM vs GD: p=0.90 and ToM vs Random: p=1).
source: Here we observed longer fixation durations for ToM animation videos (M=432.6ms) as compared to GD videos (M=279.9ms, p=0.008) and Random videos (M=308.2ms, p=0.01) for humans (p=0.029) but not for marmosets (233.7ms for ToM videos, 219.6ms for GD videos and 235.6ms for Random videos, ToM vs GD: p=0.90 and ToM vs Random: p=1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: The finding confirms that humans fixate longer in the ToM condition, whereas marmosets, like macaques, do not show this effect.
source: This finding confirms that humans fixate longer in the ToM condition (Klein et al., 2009), whereas marmosets, like macaques (Schafroth et al., 2021), do not show this effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's data and comparison with cited literature.

claim: There was a significant interaction between species and condition for the proportion of time spent looking at the large red triangle (F(2,40)=9.83, p<0.001, ηp2=0.330).
source: Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between species and condition for the proportion of time spent looking at the large red triangle (F(2,40)=9.83, p<0.001, ηp2p2.330).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: Both humans and marmosets spent a greater proportion of time looking at the red triangle in ToM compared to the GD and Random videos.
source: Specifically, both humans (Figure 2B left) and marmosets (Figure 2B right) spent a greater proportion of time looking at the red triangle in ToM compared to the GD and Random videos (for humans, ToM vs GD: Δ=.23, p<0.001 and ToM vs Random: Δ=0.31, p<0.001; for marmosets, ToM vs GD: Δ=0.13, p<0.01 and ToM vs Random: Δ=0.13, p<0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Humans allocated a greater proportion of time to the red triangle in GD compared to Random animations (Δ=0.08, p=0.05).
source: However, while humans also allocated a greater proportion of time to the red triangle in GD compared to Random animations (Δ=0.08, p=0.05), marmosets did not show any difference between these two conditions (Δ=0.0003, p=1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: Marmosets did not show any difference in proportion of time looking at the red triangle between GD and Random conditions (Δ=0.0003, p=1).
source: However, while humans also allocated a greater proportion of time to the red triangle in GD compared to Random animations (Δ=0.08, p=0.05), marmosets did not show any difference between these two conditions (Δ=0.0003, p=1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: There was a significant interaction of species and condition for the small blue triangle (F(2,40)=3.54, p=0.04, ηp2=0.151).
source: For the small blue triangle, we also observed a significant interaction of species and condition (F(2,40)=3.54, p=0.04, ηp2p2.151) but no significant pairwise differences were observed following Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: No significant pairwise differences were observed for the small blue triangle following Bonferroni correction.
source: For the small blue triangle, we also observed a significant interaction of species and condition (F(2,40)=3.54, p=0.04, ηp2p2.151) but no significant pairwise differences were observed following Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: Humans and marmosets spent the same proportion of time looking at the blue triangle in the three different types of videos.
source: Therefore, humans and marmosets spent the same proportion of time looking at the blue triangle in the three different types of videos (for humans, ToM vs GD: Δ=-0.02, p=1, ToM vs Random: Δ=0.04, p=1 and GD vs Random: Δ=0.07, p=0.23; for marmosets, ToM vs GD: Δ=-0.05, p=0.89, ToM vs Random: Δ=0.07, p=0.66 and GD vs Random: Δ=-0.02, p=1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye-tracking data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Humans show a gradient of proportion of time spent looking at the red triangle across the three conditions, with the smallest proportion in Random videos and the greatest proportion in ToM videos.
source: Notably, humans show a gradient of proportion of time spent looking at the red triangle across the three conditions, with the smallest proportion in Random videos and the greatest proportion in ToM videos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eye-tracking data patterns.

claim: Marmosets exhibit a different pattern, spending more time looking at the red triangle in ToM videos, but allocating the same proportion of time to look at the red triangle in both Random and GD videos.
source: In contrast, marmosets exhibit a different pattern, spending more time looking at the red triangle in ToM videos, but allocating the same proportion of time to look at the red triangle in both Random and GD videos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eye-tracking data patterns.

claim: Marmosets process the Random and GD conditions in a similar manner, but their processing of the ToM condition is distinct.
source: This suggests that marmosets process the Random and GD conditions in a similar manner, but their processing of the ToM condition is distinct, indicating a differential response to stimuli representing social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the eye-tracking data patterns.

claim: Both ToM and Random videos activated a large bilateral network in humans.
source: Both ToM (Figure 3A) and Random (Figure 3B) videos activated a large bilateral network.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The activated areas in humans included visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V3CD, V3B, V4, V4T, V6A, V7, MT, MST), lateral occipital areas 1, 2, and 3 (LO1, LO2, LO3), temporal areas (FST, PH, PHT, TE2, posterior inferotemporal complex PIT and fusiform face complex FFC), temporo-parietal junction areas (TPOJ2 and TPOJ3), lateral posterior parietal areas also comprising the parietal operculum (supramarginal areas PF, PFt, angular areas PGp and PGi, superior temporal visual area STV, perisylvian language area PSL, medial intraparietal area MIP, ventral and dorsal lateral intraparietal areas LIPv and LIPd, anterior intraparietal area AIP, IPS1, IPS0, 7PC and 5 L), medial superior parietal areas (7am, PCV, 5 mv), secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), premotor areas (6, 55b, premotor eye field PEF, frontal eye field FEF), and frontal areas (8Av, 8 C, IFJp, IFIa).
source: The activated areas included visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V3CD, V3B, V4, V4T, V6A, V7, MT, MST), lateral occipital areas 1, 2, and 3 (LO1, LO2, LO3), temporal areas (FST, PH, PHT, TE2, posterior inferotemporal complex PIT and fusiform face complex FFC), temporo-parietal junction areas (TPOJ2 and TPOJ3), lateral posterior parietal areas also comprising the parietal operculum (supramarginal areas PF, PFt, angular areas PGp and PGi, superior temporal visual area STV, perisylvian language area PSL, medial intraparietal area MIP, ventral and dorsal lateral intraparietal areas LIPv and LIPd, anterior intraparietal area AIP, IPS1, IPS0, 7PC and 5 L), medial superior parietal areas (7am, PCV, 5 mv), secondary somatosensory cortex (S2), premotor areas (6, 55b, premotor eye field PEF, frontal eye field FEF), and frontal areas (8Av, 8 C, IFJp, IFIa).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis identifying activated brain regions.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed bilateral activations in posterior superior temporal sulcus (STSdp), in temporo-parietal junction area TPOJ1, in ventral visual complex (VVC), in parahippocampal area 3 (PHA3), in lateral posterior parietal areas Pfop and PFcm, in lateral prefrontal areas 8 C, 8Av, 44 and 45, in inferior frontal areas IFSp, IFSa, and in frontal opercular area 5 (FOP5).
source: The ToM condition (Figure 3A) also showed bilateral activations in posterior superior temporal sulcus (STSdp), in temporo-parietal junction area TPOJ1, in ventral visual complex (VVC), in parahippocampal area 3 (PHA3), in lateral posterior parietal areas Pfop and PFcm, in lateral prefrontal areas 8 C, 8Av, 44 and 45, in inferior frontal areas IFSp, IFSa, and in frontal opercular area 5 (FOP5).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The ToM condition compared to Random condition in humans reveals increased activations in occipital, temporal, parietal and frontal areas.
source: This analysis reveals increased activations for the ToM condition compared to the Random condition in occipital, temporal, parietal and frontal areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed greater activations in bilateral visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3CD, V4, V4t, MT, MST, as well as the bilateral LO1, LO2 and LO3 regions compared to Random condition.
source: This includes notable differences in the bilateral visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3CD, V4, V4t, MT, MST, as well as the bilateral LO1, LO2 and LO3 regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed greater activations in the lateral temporal lobe, including bilateral PH and FST areas, and in the inferior temporal lobe in bilateral TE2, FFC, and PIT areas compared to Random condition.
source: The increase extends into the lateral temporal lobe, as observed in the bilateral PH and FST areas and into the more inferior part of the temporal lobe in the bilateral TE2, FFC, and PIT areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed greater activations in bilateral temporo-parietal junction areas (TPOJ1, TPOJ2, TPOJ3), and along the right STS in STSdp and STSda areas compared to Random condition.
source: We also found greater activations in the bilateral temporo-parietal junction areas (TPOJ1, TPOJ2, TPOJ3), and along the right STS in STSdp and STSda areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed greater activations in left and right parietal areas, especially in the inferior parietal lobule, including the right supramarginal and opercular supramarginal areas (PF, PFm, PFt, Pfop, and PFcm), left PFt, bilateral opercular areas PSL and STV, bilateral angular areas PGp and Pgi, right IPS1, and bilateral IP0, as well as in the superior parietal lobule (right AIP) compared to Random condition.
source: This extended to left and right parietal areas, especially in the inferior parietal lobule, including the right supramarginal and opercular supramarginal areas (PF, PFm, PFt, Pfop, and PFcm), left PFt, bilateral opercular areas PSL and STV, bilateral angular areas PGp and Pgi, right IPS1, and bilateral IP0. The activation also extended into the superior parietal lobule (right AIP).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The ToM condition in humans showed greater activations in the secondary somatosensory cortex, premotor areas (6 r and PEF), lateral prefrontal areas (8 C, 44, and 45), and the inferior (IFSa, IFSp, IFJa, and IFJp) as well as the opercular (FOP5) frontal areas in the right hemisphere compared to Random condition.
source: Moving anteriorly, we observed greater activations during ToM animations in the secondary somatosensory cortex, premotor areas (6 r and PEF), lateral prefrontal areas (8 C, 44, and 45), and the inferior (IFSa, IFSp, IFJa, and IFJp) as well as the opercular (FOP5) frontal areas in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The Random condition in humans exhibited greater activations than the ToM condition predominantly within the left and right visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4) and in dorsolateral (10d and 10r bilateral), lateral (9m left) and medial frontal areas (d32 and a24 bilateral, p24 and s32 right).
source: In contrast, the Random condition exhibited greater activations, than the ToM condition predominantly within the left and right visual areas (V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4) and in dorsolateral (10d and 10r bilateral), lateral (9m left) and medial frontal areas (d32 and a24 bilateral, p24 and s32 right).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: At the subcortical level in humans, enhanced bilateral activations were observed in the cerebellum and in certain areas of the thalamus (right ventroposterior thalamus or THA-VP, and left and right dorsoanterior thalamus or THA-DA) under both ToM and Random conditions when compared to the baseline.
source: At the subcortical level (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1, left panel), we observed enhanced bilateral activations in the cerebellum and in certain areas of the thalamus (namely, the right ventroposterior thalamus or THA-VP, and the left and right dorsoanterior thalamus or THA-DA) under both ToM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left panel) and Random conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, left panel) when compared to the baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A small section of the right amygdala was engaged in the ToM condition in humans.
source: Additionally, a small section of the right amygdala was engaged in the ToM condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: In humans, more pronounced activations were observed in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum, the right amygdala and thalamus (right THA-VP, right ventroanterior thalamus or THA-VA, and left and right dorsoposterior thalamus or THA-DP) for the ToM condition compared to the Random condition.
source: We noted more pronounced activations in the posterior lobe of the cerebellum, the right amygdala and thalamus (right THA-VP, right ventroanterior thalamus or THA-VA, and left and right dorsoposterior thalamus or THA-DP) for the ToM condition compared to the Random condition (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, left panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No regions in humans showed greater activations for Random condition compared to the ToM condition at the subcortical level.
source: No regions showed greater activations for Random condition compared to the ToM condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI contrast analysis data.

claim: The study used shorter modified versions of the Frith-Happé animations (videos of 19.5 s instead of 40 s).
source: As we used shorter modified versions of the Frith-Happé animations (i.e. videos of 19.5 s instead of 40 s), we also validated our stimuli and our fMRI protocol by comparing the brain responses elicited by ToM animation videos – compared to Random animation videos – obtained in our group of 10 human subjects and those reported by the large group of humans (496) used in the social cognition task of the Human Connectome Project (HCP; Barch et al., 2013), which also used shortened versions of the Frith-Happé animations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and validation approach.

claim: The study validated stimuli and fMRI protocol by comparing brain responses with those from the Human Connectome Project (HCP; Barch et al., 2013).
source: As we used shorter modified versions of the Frith-Happé animations (i.e. videos of 19.5 s instead of 40 s), we also validated our stimuli and our fMRI protocol by comparing the brain responses elicited by ToM animation videos – compared to Random animation videos – obtained in our group of 10 human subjects and those reported by the large group of humans (496) used in the social cognition task of the Human Connectome Project (HCP; Barch et al., 2013), which also used shortened versions of the Frith-Happé animations.
evidence: This is a description of the validation approach using comparison with HCP data.

claim: Similar distinct patterns of brain activations were observed between the current study and the HCP dataset, including a set of areas in occipital, temporal, parietal and frontal cortices.
source: Overall, we observed similar distinct patterns of brain activations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), including a set of areas in occipital, temporal, parietal and frontal cortices, as described previously (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of fMRI data with HCP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The main differences between the current study and HCP dataset were stronger activations in the left hemisphere in the HCP dataset.
source: The main differences were stronger activations in the left hemisphere in the HCP dataset.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of fMRI data with HCP data.

claim: The stimuli and protocol used in the study are appropriate to investigate mental state attribution to animated moving shapes.
source: Therefore, these results show that our stimuli and our protocol are appropriate to investigate mental state attribution to animated moving shapes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation comparison with HCP data.

claim: Both the ToM and Random animations activated an extensive network in marmosets involving a variety of areas in the occipito-temporal, parietal and frontal regions.
source: Both the ToM (Figure 4A) and Random (Figure 4B) animations activated an extensive network involving a variety of areas in the occipito-temporal, parietal and frontal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In marmosets, activations in the occipital and temporal cortex were located in the visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4, V4t, V5, V6, MST, the medial (19 M), and dorsointermediate parts (19DI) of area 19, ventral temporal area TH, enthorinal cortex, and lateral and inferior temporal areas TE3 and TEO.
source: In the occipital and temporal cortex, the activations were located in the visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3A, V4, V4t, V5, V6, MST, the medial (19 M), and dorsointermediate parts (19DI) of area 19, ventral temporal area TH, enthorinal cortex, and lateral and inferior temporal areas TE3 and TEO.
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis identifying activated brain regions in marmosets.

claim: In marmosets, activations were observed in the posterior parietal cortex, specifically in bilateral regions surrounding the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), in areas LIP, MIP, PE, PG, PFG, PF, V6A, PEC, in the occipito-parietal transitional area (OPt) and in medial part of the parietal cortex (area PGM).
source: Activations were also observed in the posterior parietal cortex, specifically in bilateral regions surrounding the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), in areas LIP, MIP, PE, PG, PFG, PF, V6A, PEC, in the occipito-parietal transitional area (OPt) and in medial part of the parietal cortex (area PGM).
evidence: This claim is supported by fMRI data analysis identifying activated brain regions in marmosets.

claim: Six marmosets (four females - weight 315–442 g, age 30–34 months - and two males - weight 374–425 g, age 30 and 55 months) were implanted with an MRI-compatible machined PEEK head post.
source: Six of these animals (four females - weight 315–442 g, age 30–34 months - and two males - weight 374–425 g, age 30 and 55 months) were implanted with an MRI-compatible machined PEEK head post (Gilbert et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a description of the study subjects and methods.

claim: Eleven healthy humans (4 females, 25–42 years, mean age: 30.7 years) participated in the eye tracking experiment.
source: Eleven healthy humans (4 females, 25–42 years, mean age: 30.7 years) participated in the eye tracking experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study subjects.

claim: Among the eleven humans in the eye tracking experiment, five individuals, along with five additional subjects (4 females, 26–45 years), took part in the fMRI experiment.
source: Among these, five individuals, along with five additional subjects (4 females, 26–45 years), took part in the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a description of the study subjects.

claim: All human subjects self-reported as right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
source: All subjects self-reported as right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and had no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is a description of the study subjects' characteristics.

claim: All human subjects confirmed they had not previously been exposed to the Frith-Happé animation videos used in the study.
source: Importantly, all subjects confirmed they had not previously been exposed to the Frith-Happé animation videos used in our study.
evidence: This is a description of the study subjects' characteristics.

claim: The original social animation task included three conditions: ToM, Goal-Directed (GD), and Random.
source: The original social animation task included three conditions: ToM, Goal-Directed (GD), and Random.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The study modified the original video clips and shortened each animation to 19.5 s using custom video-editing software (iMovie, Apple Incorporated, CA).
source: Similar to the approach used in the HCP study (Barch et al., 2013), we modified the original video clips and shortened each animation to 19.5 s using custom video-editing software (iMovie, Apple Incorporated, CA).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The percentage of time spent in each run looking at the screen in the two experimental conditions (ToM, Random) and during the Baseline periods was higher than 85% (88.2%, 88.6% and 93.4% respectively) in marmosets.
source: The percentage of time spent in each run looking at the screen in the two experimental conditions (ToM, Random) and during the Baseline periods (fixation point in the center of the screen) was higher than 85% (88.2%, 88.6% and 93.4% respectively for ToM, Random and Baseline conditions).
evidence: This is a description of behavioral compliance data from marmosets.

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage of time looking at the screen between the ToM and Random condition in marmosets (paired t-test, t(14)=-0.374, p=0.71).
source: There was no significant differences between the ToM and Random condition (paired t-test, t(14)=-0.374, p=0.71), ruling out the possibility that any differences in fMRI activation between the ToM and Random condition were simply due to a different exposure to the videos.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral compliance data.

claim: The lack of difference in screen viewing time rules out the possibility that any differences in fMRI activation between the ToM and Random condition were simply due to a different exposure to the videos in marmosets.
source: There was no significant differences between the ToM and Random condition (paired t-test, t(14)=-0.374, p=0.71), ruling out the possibility that any differences in fMRI activation between the ToM and Random condition were simply due to a different exposure to the videos.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral compliance data analysis.

claim: Marmoset fMRI data were acquired on a 9.4T 31 cm horizontal bore magnet with specific technical parameters.
source: For marmoset subjects, fMRI data were acquired on a 9.4T 31 cm horizontal bore magnet (Varian) with a Bruker BioSpec Avance III HD console running software package Paravision-360 (Bruker BioSpin Corp), a custom-built high-performance 15 cm diameter gradient coil (maximum gradient strength: 1.5 mT/m/A), and an eight-channel receive coil.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and equipment.

claim: Human fMRI data were acquired on a 7T 68 cm MRI scanner with specific technical parameters.
source: For human subjects, fMRI data were acquired on a 7T 68 cm MRI scanner (Siemens Magnetom 7T MRI Plus) with an AC-84 Mark II gradient coil, an in-house 8-channel parallel transmit, and a 32-channel receive coil (Gilbert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods and equipment.

claim: The mean tSNR calculated within peripheral brain regions nearest the coil elements is 10% higher for right hemisphere than tSNR produced by left hemisphere in humans.
source: The mean tSNR calculated within peripheral brain regions nearest the coil elements is 10% higher for right hemisphere than tSNR produced by left hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by technical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
